However, both reports have been criticised and, while some guidelines recommend the use of aspirin,8 oth- ers suggest it should not be used alone since other methods are generally more effective.11 Long-term use of low-dose aspirin appears to have little effect on the incidence of ve- nous thromboembolism.31 Direct thrombin inhibitors have been tried.32 Desirudin has been shown to be effective and was reported to be superior to both low-dose subcutaneous heparin and to a low-molecular-weight heparin in patients undergoing hip replacement surgery. Bivalirudin has also been tried. Dabigatran, an oral direct thrombin inhibitor, is effective33 and may be used in patients having hip or knee replace- ment. The direct inhibitor of factor Xa, fondaparinux, a synthet- ic pentasaccharide, has been reported34 to be more effec- tive than low-molecular-weight heparin for orthopaedic surgery, and may be used as an alternative,9-11 although bleeding may be increased. Extended prophylaxis may be of benefit.35 Rivaroxaban, an oral factor Xa inhibitor, has also been tried.36 Of the other drugs tried for surgical thromboembolism prophylaxis, dihydroergotamine can reduce venous stasis by vasoconstriction of capacitance vessels and has en- hanced postoperative prophylaxis when used with low- dose heparin, but there is a risk of peripheral ischaemia and it is no longer widely used. Dextrans (dextran 70 or dex- tran 40) alone, or with dihydroergotamine, have also been used for prophylaxis, but their use involves the infusion of 500 to 1000 mL of fluid, a procedure which is cumber- some and may interfere with fluid balance. In non-surgical patients, meta-analyses37,38 have con- firmed that anticoagulant prophylaxis reduces the risk of symptomatic venous thromboembolism, but it is less clear which patients require treatment.39 Use of low-dose sub- cutaneous heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin should be considered in patients at high risk;8,11 low- molecular-weight heparin may be preferred.9 Patients with cancer are at particular risk;40 one study41 showed that very-low-dose warfarin (average daily dose of 2.6 mg) was safe and effective in patients given chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer. Prophylaxis with low-molecular- weight heparin has been shown to be effective in patients with immobilisation of the leg,42 and in acutely ill medical patients with risk factors for venous thromboembo- lism.43,44 Standard unfractionated heparin prophylaxis, however, had no effect on mortality in patients admitted to hospital with infection.45 A study46 in older medical pa- tients found that fondaparinux may be effective.
